title: Social interactions, ethnicity, religion, and fertility in Kenya
design_class: structural/econometric GMM social-interactions model (Manski endogenous/exogenous/correlated decomposition made non-linear via Poisson/GMM) with quasi-experimental IV — mean rainfall and rainfall seasonality (District Rainfall Seasonality index) instrument the endogenous conformist effect
exposure: two diffusion terms: (1) endogenous conformist effect = deviation of own children-ever-born from the mean CEB of other women in the same village cluster / ethnic group (social contagion in fertility norms); (2) exogenous interaction = mean education of other women in the cluster; plus ethnicity and religion group membership
outcome: children ever born (CEB) / completed fertility (analysis restricted to women aged 30-49)
effect_estimate: Endogenous conformist effects positive and significant (Table 8, spec III, coefficient with IRR): Kikuyu 0.237*** (IRR 1.267), Kamba 0.221** (1.247), Kalenjin 0.190** (1.209), Luhya 0.179* (1.196), Kissi 0.159*** (1.172), Luo 0.123* (1.131) — i.e. a one-unit rise in the group-mean fertility deviation raises expected CEB by ~13-27%. Ethnic effects (Table 8 III) relative to Kikuyu: Luo 0.279** (1.321), Luhya 0.240** (1.272), Kalenjin 0.200** (1.221). Exogenous (ethnic-level education) effects mostly insignificant.
effect_se_or_ci: Reported as p-values under each coefficient (not SEs). Conformist effects (Table 8 III): Kikuyu p=0.000, Kamba p=0.003, Kalenjin p=0.003, Luhya p=0.011, Kissi p=0.000, Luo p=0.049. Standard errors robust to intra-cluster correlation. Overidentification: J-stat 7.803 (p=0.253) Table 8, 7.493 (p=0.278) Table 10 (pass); religion-only model J=19.046 (p=0.004) fails.
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: partial — the paper explicitly confronts Manski's reflection problem and separates the endogenous social-interaction (conformist) effect from exogenous/correlated effects using (a) the non-linearity of the Poisson/GMM conditional mean and (b) rainfall mean & seasonality as excluded instruments, validated with a J-test; identification still rests on functional-form and the exclusion restriction (rainfall may affect fertility through income/agriculture beyond the modeled channel).
setting_sample: Kenya, 1998 Kenya DHS (TFR ~4.7); 5,994 rural women aged 15-49 (completed-fertility analysis restricted to 30-49) across 6 main ethnic groups and 3 religions; matched to 1930-2000 monthly rainfall from 31 meteorological stations.
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — core estimand is the social-interaction/social-learning effect of socially proximate others' fertility (village-cluster and ethnic-group peers) on own completed fertility; the endogenous conformist effect is precisely peer adoption raising/lowering own fertility. Not A.20 (models the substantive fertility norm, not a content-agnostic media/network-architecture channel); religion (A.6/D.1-adjacent) effects tested and found largely insignificant, so it is not primarily a religion paper.
risk_of_bias: moderate — main threat: identification of the endogenous effect relies on the rainfall exclusion restriction and on non-linear functional form; residual confounding/correlated effects possible, and the religion specification fails the overidentification test (though the ethnicity specifications pass).
notes: All estimates are full-text (Tables 8-10). This is the strongest-identified of the three PDFs: it directly targets the reflection problem with an instrument. Kikuyu (lowest-fertility group) show the strongest endogenous/conformist effect, consistent with social multipliers sustaining a low-fertility norm; conformity is symmetric (amplifies whichever norm prevails), hence direction coded mixed. Coefficients are proportional changes in CEB; IRRs shown in tables.
